title: Capping concurrent async calls
question: A partner API allows at most 4 concurrent requests. Many callers run `await client.GetAsync(...)` at the same time and you must cap in-flight calls at 4. Which primitive fits best?
options: A `lock` statement around the await, using a shared gate object
A `SemaphoreSlim(4, 4)` with `await WaitAsync()` and `Release()` in finally
A `Mutex` acquired with WaitOne before each call and released after it
`Interlocked.Increment` on a counter, skipping the call when it exceeds 4
explanation: SemaphoreSlim counts up to N holders and supports asynchronous waiting via WaitAsync; releasing in finally prevents permanently leaking a slot. A lock admits one holder and cannot contain an await, a Mutex has thread affinity (the continuation after await may run on another thread) and is heavyweight, and an Interlocked counter that skips calls drops work instead of queueing it.

title: Stop flag never observed in Release
question: A worker thread runs `while (!_stop) { counter++; }` where `_stop` is a plain bool field. Another thread later sets `_stop = true`. In a Release build the loop sometimes never ends. What is the cause and fix?
options: The JIT may hoist the read of `_stop` out of the loop; use Volatile.Read or volatile
Bool writes are not atomic in .NET, so the field tears; set it via Interlocked.Exchange
The writer's store sits in its CPU store buffer forever; call GC.Collect to flush it
Release builds drop writes to fields read only by other threads; disable optimization
explanation: Without volatile semantics the JIT may assume no other thread changes the field, read it once into a register and turn the loop into an infinite one. Volatile.Read, the volatile keyword or a CancellationToken forces a fresh read on each iteration. Bool writes are atomic, store buffers drain on their own, and the compiler does not remove the writer's assignment.

title: Nondestructive mutation with `with`
options: Compile error: positional records are immutable
explanation: A `with` expression creates a copy of the record with the listed properties changed, leaving the original untouched, so p1 keeps 30 and p2 gets 31. Init-only properties of positional records can be set inside a `with` initializer, so it compiles.

title: `with` makes a shallow copy
options: 1, because `with` deep-clones every reference-type member of the record
1, because records snapshot collections into immutable arrays on creation
2, because `with` copies member values, so both records share one List
Compile error, because a record's List member cannot be mutated after init
explanation: `with` performs a shallow copy: reference-type members are copied as references, so a and b point at the same List and the Add is visible through both. Records do not deep-clone or freeze collections, and init-only only prevents reassigning the property, not mutating the object it refers to.

title: Struct arrays ignore constructors
explanation: `new Config()` runs the explicit parameterless constructor, which executes the field initializer, so Retries is 3. Creating an array of structs (like `default(Config)`) ignores constructors and fills elements with the zero bit pattern, so each element's Retries is 0.

title: Abstract member left unimplemented
options: Error: Circle must override Area() or be declared abstract itself
It compiles; Circle.Area() throws NotImplementedException when called
It compiles; Circle inherits an Area() that returns 0 by default
Error: abstract classes cannot declare methods that lack a body
explanation: A non-abstract class deriving from an abstract class must override every inherited abstract member (error CS0534), or itself be marked abstract. Abstract methods have no body by definition and there is no default implementation or runtime stub.

title: Calling an explicit interface implementation
options: It compiles and calls ILogger.Log, as for any implemented member
It compiles but throws MissingMethodException at runtime
Compile error: interface members must be implemented as public methods
Compile error: an explicit implementation is callable only via ILogger
explanation: Explicitly implemented members are not part of the class's public surface; you call them through the interface, e.g. `((ILogger)f).Log("hi")` or a variable typed as ILogger. Explicit implementation is a valid alternative to a public method, and the failure is at compile time, not at runtime.

title: Overriding a sealed override
options: It compiles; sealed only prevents classes from deriving from B
It compiles, but C.Run() is never reached through an A reference
Compile error: C cannot override Run because B sealed it
Compile error: sealed is only valid on classes, not on methods
explanation: `sealed` combined with `override` stops further overriding of that member in derived classes, so C's override is error CS0239 (C could only hide it with `new`). Sealing a method is valid, and it does not prevent deriving from B itself.

title: Constraint for `new T()`
question: Inside `static T Create<T>()`, which constraint lets you write `return new T();`?
options: where T : class
where T : new()
where T : notnull
where T : ICloneable
explanation: The new() constraint requires a public parameterless constructor, which is what `new T()` needs. `class` only requires a reference type (which may lack such a constructor), `notnull` only excludes nullable types, and an interface constraint says nothing about constructors.

title: Unconstrained T? with a value type
options: int holding 0, since unconstrained T? is just T for value types
int? holding null, because T? always means Nullable<T> here
object holding null, because T? boxes value-type arguments
Compile error: T? is only legal when T has a class or struct constraint
explanation: For an unconstrained type parameter, T? is a nullability annotation: it means a nullable reference for reference types but plain T for value types, so `default` yields 0. This is why Enumerable.FirstOrDefault (declared to return TSource?) returns 0 for an empty List<int>. Getting Nullable<int> requires a `struct` constraint, and unconstrained T? has been legal since C# 9.

title: Arithmetic in generic code
question: You want one method `T Sum<T>(IEnumerable<T> xs)` that uses `T.Zero` and the `+` operator and works for int, double and decimal. Which approach does .NET 7+ support directly?
options: Constrain `where T : struct` so the compiler allows arithmetic operators
Constrain `where T : IComparable<T>`, which exposes operators and Zero
Cast each value to `dynamic` inside the loop; generics can't use operators
Constrain `where T : INumber<T>`, using static abstract interface members
explanation: Generic math (.NET 7 / C# 11) defines interfaces such as INumber<TSelf> with static abstract members like Zero and operator +, which the built-in numeric types implement. A struct constraint grants no operators, IComparable<T> only provides CompareTo, and `dynamic` works but is slow and not type-safe; generics can now use operators through these interfaces.

title: Why generic value-type calls avoid boxing
question:
static bool Less<T>(T a, T b) where T : IComparable<T> => a.CompareTo(b) < 0;

Profiling shows `Less<int>` allocates nothing, while a non-generic version taking `IComparable` parameters boxed every int. Why does the generic version avoid boxing?
options: The C# compiler emits a separate IL copy of Less for every value type it is called with
The runtime caches one boxed int per distinct value and reuses it for each CompareTo call
The JIT emits a specialized native body per value type and calls CompareTo directly
Generic methods run in the interpreter tier, which unboxes value-type arguments for free
explanation: The IL for Less exists once; at run time the CLR generates specialized native code for each value-type instantiation (reference types share one canonical version). In the int-specialized code, the constrained interface call binds straight to Int32.CompareTo with no box. There is no per-value box cache and .NET does not interpret generic methods.

title: Matching a method to Func/Action
question: Which delegate type matches a method `string Format(int value)`?
options: Action<int, string>
Func<int, string>
Func<string, int>
Predicate<int>
explanation: In Func, the last type argument is the return type and the preceding ones are parameters, so Func<int, string> takes an int and returns a string. Action delegates return void, Predicate<int> returns bool, and Func<string, int> has the types reversed.

title: Return value of a multicast delegate
options: Compile error: Func cannot be combined with +=
explanation: Combining delegates builds an invocation list; invoking it calls every target in order, and the result of the call is the return value of the last one, so 3 is printed. Results are not summed, and += works for any delegate type. To collect every result, iterate GetInvocationList().

title: Exception in one event handler
question: An event has three subscribers. During `Changed?.Invoke(this, EventArgs.Empty)` the second handler throws. What happens to the third handler, and how can a publisher isolate failures?
options: It still runs, because the runtime invokes each handler inside its own try/catch
It runs on the thread pool, because a failing handler moves the rest off the caller
It runs first next time, since a throwing handler is moved to the end of the list
It never runs; iterate GetInvocationList() and invoke each handler in a try/catch
explanation: A multicast delegate calls its targets sequentially on the caller's thread; an exception propagates immediately and the remaining targets are skipped. A publisher that must notify everyone can iterate GetInvocationList() and wrap each call in try/catch. The runtime adds no per-handler protection and never reorders or reschedules handlers.

title: OrderBy followed by OrderBy
question:
var sorted = people
    .OrderBy(p => p.LastName)
    .OrderBy(p => p.FirstName)
    .ToList();

The intent was 'by last name, then first name'. What does LINQ to Objects actually produce?
options: Sorted by LastName then FirstName, the same as using ThenBy for the second key
Sorted by FirstName only, with ties in arbitrary order since the first sort is lost
Sorted by FirstName, with ties ordered by LastName because OrderBy is stable
An InvalidOperationException, because OrderBy cannot follow another OrderBy
explanation: The second OrderBy starts a new primary sort on FirstName. Because Enumerable.OrderBy is a stable sort, elements with equal first names keep the LastName order from the first pass, so the keys end up reversed from the intent. Use OrderBy(LastName).ThenBy(FirstName) for a secondary key.

title: What the null-forgiving operator does
options: It throws ArgumentNullException at the assignment
Nothing: it only silences the compiler's nullable warning
It replaces null with an empty string automatically
It throws a NullReferenceException right at the assignment
explanation: The null-forgiving operator is purely a compile-time annotation that suppresses nullable warnings; it emits no check. `display` simply becomes null, and any failure happens later when it is dereferenced. Use a real null check or `?? ""` when null is possible.

title: Order of catch clauses
options: Compile error: the IOException clause is unreachable after catch (Exception)
It compiles; the most specific matching catch clause is always chosen first
It compiles; IOExceptions run both catch blocks, from the top one down
It compiles with a warning, and IOException is handled by Retry() at runtime
explanation: Catch clauses are checked top to bottom and only the first match runs, so a clause for a derived type after one for its base type can never be reached; the compiler reports error CS0160. Order clauses from most specific to most general.

title: Logging from an exception filter
question:
catch (Exception ex) when (LogAndReturnFalse(ex)) { }

Why do some teams log exceptions inside a `when` filter that always returns false?
options: Filters run on a background thread, so logging there never slows the request
Returning false turns the exception into a cheap first-chance-only event
The filter swallows the exception after logging, so callers never see it at all
It logs before the stack unwinds, and the exception keeps propagating untouched
explanation: Exception filters are evaluated before the stack is unwound. Returning false means the catch block is never entered, so the exception continues to propagate with its original stack and state, which also keeps crash dumps and debuggers pointing at the throw site. Filters run synchronously on the throwing thread and do not swallow anything.

title: HashSet.Add with a duplicate
options: True True 2
True True 1
True False 1
Throws ArgumentException on the second Add
explanation: HashSet<T>.Add returns true when the element was added and false when it was already present; duplicates are silently ignored, so the count stays 1. Unlike Dictionary.Add, a duplicate does not throw.

title: Removing items inside foreach
options: Both are removed, since List<T> adjusts the enumerator after each Remove
InvalidOperationException: the collection was modified during enumeration
Only the first is removed; the enumerator silently skips the next element
It does not compile, because Remove cannot be called inside a foreach body
explanation: List<T> keeps a version number; after the first Remove, the enumerator's next MoveNext detects the change and throws InvalidOperationException. It compiles fine. Use `orders.RemoveAll(o => o.IsCancelled)` or iterate backwards with a for loop instead.

title: PriorityQueue dequeue order
options: page
email
sms
It depends on insertion order, as with Queue<T>
explanation: PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority> is a min-heap: Dequeue returns the element with the lowest priority value, here "page" with 1. It is not FIFO, and to dequeue the highest value first you pass a reversed IComparer<TPriority>.

title: Read-only lookup built once at startup
question: A service builds a 50,000-entry currency lookup once at startup and then reads it millions of times per second from many threads, never modifying it. Which choice fits best?
options: ConcurrentDictionary, since lock-free reads beat any other structure
ImmutableDictionary, since its tree layout makes lookups O(1) and cache friendly
SortedDictionary, since binary search outperforms hashing on large sets
FrozenDictionary via ToFrozenDictionary(): slower to build, faster lookups
explanation: FrozenDictionary (.NET 8+) spends extra time at creation analysing the keys to optimise lookups, and being immutable it is safe for concurrent reads, which is ideal for build-once, read-many data. ConcurrentDictionary pays for supporting writes, ImmutableDictionary is a balanced tree with O(log n) lookups, and SortedDictionary is also O(log n).

title: Why finalizable objects live longer
question: A profiler shows that short-lived objects of a class with a finalizer (`~Wrapper()`) reach gen 1 and gen 2 far more often than similar classes without one. Why?
options: Finalizable objects are allocated directly in gen 2 so they live long enough
The finalizer pins the object, preventing the GC from compacting or collecting it
When found dead they wait for the finalizer thread, so they survive a collection
The GC scans finalizable objects only during full gen 2 collections, by design
explanation: Objects with finalizers are tracked on a finalization queue. When the GC finds one unreachable it cannot free it yet; it is kept alive (and promoted) until the finalizer thread runs, and only a later collection reclaims it. That is why classes should avoid finalizers unless they own unmanaged resources, and call GC.SuppressFinalize in Dispose.

title: GetType returns the runtime type
options: Object
String
RuntimeType
Char[]
explanation: GetType returns the exact runtime type of the instance, not the static type of the variable, so a string stored in an object variable reports String. `typeof(object)` would give Object; RuntimeType is the internal class of the Type object itself, not of the instance.

title: Applying an attribute to the wrong target
options: Compile error: the attribute is not valid on this declaration type
It compiles; AttributeUsage is only a hint for documentation tools
It compiles, and the attribute is applied to every method of the class
It compiles, but GetCustomAttributes throws when reading the class
explanation: AttributeUsage restricts where an attribute may be applied, and the compiler enforces it (error CS0592). It is not merely documentation, and the compiler never propagates a class-level attribute onto members.

title: GetField and non-public members
options: False; GetField searches all fields regardless of their access modifier
False, but reading it later throws FieldAccessException from outside the class
True; private fields are removed from metadata by the compiler in Release builds
True; GetField() defaults to public members, so pass NonPublic | Instance
explanation: The single-argument GetField overload searches only public instance and static fields. To find `_balance` you call GetField("_balance", BindingFlags.NonPublic | BindingFlags.Instance). Private fields remain in metadata in every build configuration.

title: Speeding up reflection on a hot path
question: A serializer calls `prop.GetMethod!.Invoke(obj, null)` for every property of millions of objects, and MethodInfo.Invoke dominates the CPU profile. Which change usually helps the most?
options: Call Type.GetProperties() again before each Invoke so lookups stay fresh
Wrap Invoke in a lock so the runtime can reuse its internal argument arrays
Create a typed delegate once per property with CreateDelegate and cache it
Switch to `dynamic`, which needs no metadata and removes all binding cost
explanation: MethodInfo.Invoke validates arguments and goes through a generic invocation path on every call. Creating a strongly typed delegate (e.g. Func<T, TProp>) once with CreateDelegate and caching it turns each access into a near-direct call. Re-fetching metadata adds cost, a lock only adds contention, and `dynamic` still binds through reflection and needs member names at compile time.

title: Span slices share memory
options: data[0] is 0, since Slice copies the 16 bytes into a new stack buffer
data[0] is 0xFF, since the slice is a view over the same memory
data[0] is 0, since spans are read-only unless created with stackalloc
It throws, because a span over a managed array cannot be written to
explanation: A Span<T> is a pointer plus length over existing memory; Slice just narrows that window without allocating or copying, so writes go straight into the array. Span<T> is writable over arrays (ReadOnlySpan<T> is the read-only variant).

title: stackalloc with an untrusted length
options: Possible stack overflow; stackalloc below a small threshold, else ArrayPool
None; the runtime moves large stackalloc buffers to the heap automatically
A memory leak, because stack memory is freed only when the thread exits
The GC must scan the buffer, so allocate it once in a static field instead
explanation: stackalloc reserves memory on the thread's limited stack; a large or attacker-controlled size can trigger a StackOverflowException, which cannot be caught and kills the process. The usual pattern is `len <= 256 ? stackalloc byte[len] : pooled/heap buffer`. Stack memory is released when the method returns, and the runtime never relocates it to the heap.

title: Struct dictionary keys without IEquatable
question: `struct GeoKey { public string Region; public int Cell; }` has no Equals/GetHashCode overrides and is used as a Dictionary key on a hot path. Profiling shows heavy time in ValueType.Equals plus allocations. What is the best fix?
options: Change GeoKey to a class so Dictionary uses reference equality instead
Mark the struct readonly so the runtime can compare fields bitwise
Pass the key with `in` everywhere so Dictionary can skip its defensive copies
Implement IEquatable<GeoKey> and override GetHashCode (or use record struct)
explanation: The inherited ValueType.Equals(object) boxes the argument and, for structs containing reference fields, compares fields through a slow generic path; Microsoft recommends overriding it for performance. Implementing IEquatable<T> lets EqualityComparer<T>.Default call a typed Equals with no boxing, and a record struct generates this for you. A class without overrides would break lookups by value, and readonly or `in` do not change how equality is computed.

title: What a .NET assembly contains
question: What does the C# compiler put in a .dll for a normal `dotnet build`, and what turns it into machine code?
options: Native x64 machine code; the CLR just loads and links it at startup
Compressed C# source, which the CLR compiles in full on first launch
IL and metadata; the JIT turns methods into native code at run time
Bytecode run line by line by an interpreter built into the CLR host
explanation: Roslyn emits Intermediate Language plus metadata. At run time the CLR's JIT compiler translates each method to native code (typically on first call, refined later by tiered compilation). Source is not shipped, and ahead-of-time native code only appears with options such as ReadyToRun or Native AOT.

title: Higher memory in an ASP.NET Core app
question: An ASP.NET Core API on .NET 8 running on a 16-core VM uses far more memory than a console tool processing the same data. No GC settings were changed. What is the most likely explanation?
options: ASP.NET Core disables background GC, so gen 2 collections are postponed
ASP.NET Core defaults to Server GC, which uses a heap per core
Web apps run on the 32-bit runtime by default, which fragments the heap
Kestrel pins all request buffers, so the GC can never compact the heap
explanation: ASP.NET Core apps use Server GC by default, which creates a heap and GC thread per core and lets heaps grow larger in exchange for throughput; console apps default to Workstation GC. Background GC is not disabled, apps are 64-bit by default, and Kestrel uses pooled, not permanently pinned, buffers. (.NET 9's DATAS reduces this gap by adapting the heap count.)

title: ReadyToRun code under load
question: A team publishes with `<PublishReadyToRun>true</PublishReadyToRun>` to cut cold-start time. What happens to hot methods after the app has been running under load?
options: Tiered compilation re-JITs them, because R2R code is less optimized than tier-1 code
They stay as precompiled R2R code forever, since the JIT is disabled for R2R assemblies
They switch to the interpreter, since R2R code cannot be profiled for optimization
They are recompiled by Native AOT in the background and swapped in at the next GC
explanation: ReadyToRun code avoids JIT work at startup but is less optimized than JIT output, so tiered compilation replaces frequently called R2R methods with fully optimized tier-1 code. The JIT stays enabled, there is no interpreter fallback, and Native AOT is a separate publish model, not a runtime recompiler.

title: Branch on static readonly disappears
options: Roslyn evaluates the environment variable at build time and folds the result
Dynamic PGO measured that B() was never called and deleted it permanently
static readonly fields are stored in CPU registers, so the branch is free
Tier-1 JIT runs after the static ctor, so it treats the field as a constant
explanation: With tiered compilation, the tier-1 recompile happens after the class's static constructor has run; since a static readonly value can no longer change, the JIT embeds it as a constant and removes the dead branch. Roslyn cannot know a run-time environment variable, PGO adds guarded fast paths rather than deleting code, and fields are not pinned to registers.

title: Sync scope disposal of IAsyncDisposable
options: Nothing; Exporter is never disposed and the scope leaks it silently
DisposeAsync runs fire-and-forget on the thread pool after Dispose returns
It throws InvalidOperationException; use await using + CreateAsyncScope()
DisposeAsync is blocked on synchronously, which is safe for scoped services
explanation: When a scope is disposed synchronously and it tracks a service that implements only IAsyncDisposable, the built-in container throws InvalidOperationException saying the type only implements IAsyncDisposable. Create the scope with CreateAsyncScope() and dispose it with `await using`, so DisposeAsync is awaited properly. The container neither ignores it nor fires and forgets.

title: Failing fast on invalid options
question: SmtpOptions.Port has `[Range(1, 65535)]`. A typo in appsettings leaves Port at 0; the app starts fine and only fails hours later when the first email is sent. Which registration makes it fail at startup?
options: services.Configure<SmtpOptions>(config.GetSection("Smtp")) on its own
AddOptions<SmtpOptions>().Bind(...).ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart()
Inject IOptionsMonitor<SmtpOptions> so changes are re-read on demand
Register it with services.AddSingleton(new SmtpOptions()) and bind it manually
explanation: ValidateDataAnnotations runs the attribute checks when options are created, and ValidateOnStart forces that validation while the host starts, so a bad value stops the app immediately. Plain Configure does no validation, IOptionsMonitor only changes reload behaviour, and a manually registered instance bypasses the options pipeline entirely.

title: Named options through IOptions<T>
options: IOptions<T> only exposes the unnamed instance; use IOptionsSnapshot/Monitor.Get(name)
Named options merge in registration order, so Backup's empty Host overwrote Primary
Named options are bound lazily and only after the first IOptionsMonitor change event
Section keys that contain a colon cannot be bound unless they are escaped with __
explanation: IOptions<T> does not support named options: .Value returns the default (unnamed) instance, which nothing configured here. Named instances are read with IOptionsSnapshot<T>.Get("Primary") or IOptionsMonitor<T>.Get("Primary"). Named instances are kept separate, and the colon is the normal configuration key separator (__ is only for environment variables).

title: Minimal API simple parameter binding
question:
app.MapGet("/search", (string term, int page) => ...);

With no attributes, where does ASP.NET Core bind `term` and `page` from for `GET /search?term=net&page=2`?
options: From the JSON request body, which GET requests send by default
From request headers named term and page, matched case-insensitively
From DI services, since parameters without attributes come from there
From the query string, since simple types not in the route use it
explanation: Minimal APIs infer sources: simple types such as string and int that do not match a route parameter are bound from the query string. JSON bodies are inferred only for complex types (and GET requests normally have no body), headers require [FromHeader], and only registered service types are resolved from DI.

title: Setting headers after the response started
options: Header names starting with X- are reserved; prefix custom headers differently
next() disposes HttpContext, so capture the Response object before calling it
Headers were already sent with the body; set them in Response.OnStarting(...)
Stopwatch is not thread-safe across awaits; use DateTime.UtcNow differences
explanation: Once the endpoint starts writing the body, the status line and headers are flushed and the response has started; changing headers afterwards throws. Registering a callback with Response.OnStarting runs just before headers are sent, which is the right moment to add them. X- headers are allowed, HttpContext is still valid after next(), and the Stopwatch is not the problem.

title: AllowAnonymous inside an Authorize controller
question: A controller has `[Authorize]` at class level. One action, Login, is marked `[AllowAnonymous]`. What happens when an unauthenticated user calls Login?
options: 401, because the class-level attribute always overrides action attributes
The request succeeds; AllowAnonymous skips authorization for that action
403, because anonymous users are authenticated but lack any role claims
500, because mixing Authorize and AllowAnonymous is a configuration error
explanation: [AllowAnonymous] bypasses authorization for the endpoint it decorates, even when [Authorize] is applied at the controller level, which is the standard way to expose a login action. Anonymous users are not authenticated at all, and combining the two attributes is a supported pattern.

title: Requiring a claim value
question: Only users whose token has the claim `department` = `Finance` may call the reports endpoints. What is the idiomatic ASP.NET Core way to express this?
options: A named policy built with RequireClaim("department", "Finance") on [Authorize]
Check User.Claims at the start of every action and return Forbid() if it's absent
[Authorize(Roles = "department=Finance")], since Roles also accepts claim filters
A middleware that deletes non-Finance claims before the authorization step runs
explanation: Claims-based authorization uses a policy: `options.AddPolicy("FinanceOnly", p => p.RequireClaim("department", "Finance"))` and `[Authorize(Policy = "FinanceOnly")]` on the endpoints. Manual checks scatter and duplicate the rule, Roles matches only role claims by name, and stripping claims in middleware does not enforce anything.

title: Random logouts after scaling out
question: After scaling an ASP.NET Core app that uses cookie auth from 1 to 4 container replicas behind a round-robin load balancer, users are randomly logged out, antiforgery validation fails, and every deploy logs everyone out. What is the root cause?
options: Cookies exceed the 4 KB browser limit once more replicas add their own signatures
The load balancer strips Set-Cookie headers unless sticky sessions are configured
JWT signing keys rotate on each replica start, invalidating every issued token
Each replica keeps its own Data Protection keys; persist them to shared storage
explanation: Auth cookies and antiforgery tokens are protected with the Data Protection key ring. Inside containers each replica generates its own keys in ephemeral storage, so a cookie issued by one replica cannot be decrypted by another, and redeploys discard all keys. Persist keys to shared storage (e.g. PersistKeysToAzureBlobStorage, a shared file system or Redis) and use the same SetApplicationName on every instance.

title: Registering a BackgroundService
question: You wrote `class OutboxWorker : BackgroundService`. How do you get the host to start it together with the app?
options: builder.Services.AddSingleton<OutboxWorker>(), which starts it on first use
Call new OutboxWorker().StartAsync() at the end of Program.cs after app.Run()
builder.Services.AddHostedService<OutboxWorker>()
builder.Services.AddScoped<IHostedService, OutboxWorker>() for each request
explanation: AddHostedService registers the type as an IHostedService, and the host calls StartAsync on all hosted services during startup and StopAsync on shutdown. A plain singleton is never started, code after app.Run() runs only once the app is shutting down, and hosted services are not per-request.

title: HTTP status for a Degraded check
question: A health check returns `HealthCheckResult.Degraded("cache slow")`. With default MapHealthChecks options, which HTTP status does the endpoint return?
options: 503 Service Unavailable
200 OK
500 Internal Server Error
429 Too Many Requests
explanation: By default ResultStatusCodes maps Healthy and Degraded to 200 and only Unhealthy to 503, so probes keep routing traffic to a degraded instance. You can change the mapping through HealthCheckOptions.ResultStatusCodes if Degraded should fail the probe.

title: Graceful shutdown of a queue consumer
question: A queue consumer's ExecuteAsync loops `while (true)` and calls `await handler.ProcessAsync(msg)` without passing any token. During rolling deploys Kubernetes sends SIGTERM and some messages end up half-processed. What is the right fix?
options: Loop on !stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested and pass the token to async calls
Catch SIGTERM with Console.CancelKeyPress and call Environment.Exit(0) at once
Make ExecuteAsync synchronous so the host cannot stop it partway through
Set HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout to zero so the host stops before new work begins
explanation: On SIGTERM the host begins graceful shutdown and signals the stoppingToken passed to ExecuteAsync, then waits up to HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout for it to finish. Honouring the token lets the worker stop taking new messages and finish or abandon the current one cleanly. Exiting immediately or a zero timeout makes interruption worse, and blocking code just ignores shutdown.

title: Long-lived DbContext returns stale data
question: A worker reuses one DbContext for hours. Another app updates Product 7's price, but `await db.Products.FirstAsync(p => p.Id == 7)` in the worker keeps returning the old price. Why?
options: EF Core caches query results for 24 hours unless AsNoTracking is applied
FirstAsync reads from the change tracker only, never from the database
SQL Server keeps returning the cached plan's results until the connection pool resets
The row is queried, but EF returns the tracked instance without its new values
explanation: Tracking queries always execute against the database, but identity resolution means that if an entity with that key is already tracked, EF returns the existing instance and does not overwrite its values with the database values. Use a short-lived DbContext per unit of work (or AsNoTracking / Reload) to see fresh data. EF has no time-based result cache, and plan caching does not cache results.

title: Caveat of DbContext pooling
question: A high-throughput API switches from AddDbContext to `AddDbContextPool<AppDbContext>()`. What must the team be careful about?
options: Pooled contexts are shared by concurrent requests, so add locks around SaveChanges
Pooling disables change tracking, so every update must use ExecuteUpdateAsync
Custom state on the context (e.g. a tenant field set per request) is not reset
Pooled contexts keep tracked entities between requests as a 2nd-level cache
explanation: With pooling EF Core resets its own state (change tracker, etc.) when a context is returned, but the constructor runs only once per pooled instance and your own fields are not reset, so per-request state can leak between requests. Each rented context is still used by one request at a time, change tracking works normally, and tracked entities are cleared on return.

title: Data-driven tests in xUnit
question: In xUnit, you want to run the same test method for the inputs (2, 4), (3, 9) and (4, 16). Which attributes do you use?
options: [Fact] on the method, copied three times with different names
[Theory] with three [InlineData(...)] attributes on the method
[TestCase(...)] three times, which xUnit reads like NUnit does
[Fact(Repeat = 3)] plus a static array holding the input pairs
explanation: In xUnit, [Fact] marks a parameterless test and [Theory] marks a parameterised one whose data comes from [InlineData], [MemberData] or [ClassData]. [TestCase] belongs to NUnit, and Fact has no Repeat property; copying the method duplicates code.

title: Mock versus stub
question: A unit test replaces IEmailSender with a fake and then asserts that SendAsync was called exactly once with the customer's address. In the usual terminology, that fake is a:
options: Mock
Stub
Dummy
Fixture
explanation: A mock is a fake the test asserts against, so it decides whether the test passes; here the test verifies the interaction. A stub only supplies canned responses so the code under test can run, a dummy is passed but never used, and a fixture is shared setup rather than a test double.

title: Expensive setup runs for every test
question: An xUnit test class starts a PostgreSQL container in its constructor. With 20 tests in the class, the container starts 20 times and the suite takes minutes. Why, and what is the fix?
options: xUnit runs every test in a new process; enable a shared AppDomain in xunit.runner.json
Constructors run before each assertion; move setup into a static constructor instead
Tests run in parallel inside a class; add [Collection] to make them run in sequence
xUnit creates a new class instance per test; move setup into an IClassFixture<T>
explanation: xUnit deliberately creates a fresh instance of the test class for every test, so constructor setup repeats each time. A class fixture (IClassFixture<T>, optionally with IAsyncLifetime) is created once and shared by all tests in the class, or a collection fixture shares it across classes. Tests in the same class run sequentially, and xUnit does not start a process per test.

title: Testing time-dependent code
question: A TokenCache expires entries after 30 minutes using `DateTime.UtcNow`. Its tests use Thread.Sleep and are slow and flaky. What is the recommended .NET 8+ approach?
options: Mark tests [Fact(Timeout = 1800000)] so xUnit waits for the real expiry
Set the machine clock forward in test setup and restore it in Dispose()
Inject TimeProvider, use GetUtcNow(), and advance a FakeTimeProvider in tests
Replace DateTime.UtcNow with Stopwatch.GetTimestamp(), which tests can freeze at will
explanation: TimeProvider (.NET 8) abstracts the clock and timers; production code injects TimeProvider.System, while tests use FakeTimeProvider from Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing and call Advance to move time instantly and deterministically. Waiting in real time is slow, changing the machine clock affects everything else, and Stopwatch timestamps cannot be frozen by tests.
